definitions.definition: When parts of a system are aligned and working together smoothly, like a perfectly tuned choir.
definitions.example: A laser beam is coherent because all its light waves are in step.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to get messier over time.
definitions.example: Your bedroom naturally gets messier (higher entropy) unless you put energy into cleaning it.

definitions.definition: The process where a system loses its organized, wave-like behavior and becomes random and classical.
definitions.example: When you drop a quantum coin, it stops being both heads and tails and becomes just one or the other.

definitions.definition: A symbol used in this framework to represent the overall coherence or order of a system.
definitions.example: Think of χ as a score from -1 to +1 that tells you how organized something is.

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula that describes how a system changes over time, especially in quantum physics.
definitions.example: It's like a recipe that tells you how the ingredients of a system will mix and change.

definitions.definition: A Greek letter used here as a symbol for the coherence value, ranging from +1 (perfect order) to -1 (perfect disorder).
definitions.example: If σ = +1, everything is perfectly aligned; if σ = -1, everything is chaotic.

definitions.definition: Different ways of looking at or measuring the same thing, like using a ruler vs. a scale to describe an object.
definitions.example: A doctor and a physicist might measure the same fever using different tools and terms.

definitions.definition: A judgment about whether something is good or bad, right or wrong, based on a standard.
definitions.example: Saying 'stealing is wrong' is a normative assessment.

definitions.definition: Signal-to-noise ratio, measured in decibels; how much clear information there is compared to random interference.
definitions.example: A good radio station has high SNR because the music is clear and the static is low.

definitions.definition: When waves or cycles are synchronized so their peaks and troughs match up.
definitions.example: Two pendulums swinging in perfect sync have phase alignment.

definitions.definition: When the parts of something fit together in a pleasing, balanced way.
definitions.example: A well-designed building has structural harmony because all its parts work together nicely.

definitions.definition: Heart rate variability; the natural variation in time between heartbeats, a sign of health.
definitions.example: A healthy person has some HRV because their heart speeds up and slows down naturally.

definitions.definition: Substances in the blood that show how well the immune system is working.
definitions.example: Doctors check immune markers to see if you have an infection.

definitions.definition: When the parts of an organization (like a government or company) work together smoothly and fairly.
definitions.example: A school with clear rules and good communication has institutional coherence.

definitions.definition: When relationships are healthy, honest, and aligned with mutual care.
definitions.example: A friendship where both people trust and support each other has relational coherence.

definitions.definition: Being connected to the divine order or logic of the universe, often associated with God's plan.
definitions.example: In some beliefs, praying is a way to strengthen Logos coupling.

definitions.definition: Being in harmony with the fundamental coherence field (χ) that underlies reality.
definitions.example: Acting with kindness might increase your χ-field alignment.

definitions.definition: How well something holds together without breaking or falling apart.
definitions.example: A bridge with good structural integrity can support heavy loads without collapsing.

definitions.definition: The flow of order or negative entropy into a system, keeping it organized and alive.
definitions.example: Eating food provides negentropy flux to your body, keeping you alive and organized.

definitions.definition: The number of independent ways a system can move or change.
definitions.example: A ball on a table has two degrees of freedom: it can move left/right and forward/backward.

definitions.definition: The maximum amount of information that can be sent through a communication channel without error.
definitions.example: A fiber optic cable has a high channel capacity, so it can carry lots of data.

definitions.definition: When two or more waves have the same frequency and are in sync.
definitions.example: Two tuning forks that vibrate at the same pitch have frequency alignment.

definitions.definition: When different parts of the brain fire in sync, leading to calm, focused thinking.
definitions.example: Meditation can increase neural coherence, helping you feel peaceful.

definitions.definition: The movement of goods, money, or energy through a system.
definitions.example: A healthy economy has a steady resource flow from producers to consumers.

definitions.definition: The idea that what is right or wrong depends on a person's culture, beliefs, or situation, not on universal rules.
definitions.example: Someone who says 'stealing is okay in some cultures' is expressing moral relativism.

definitions.definition: A law of physics that says disorder (entropy) in a closed system always increases over time.
definitions.example: An ice cube melts into a puddle because the Second Law says order decreases.

definitions.definition: The study of where words come from and how their meanings have changed over time.
definitions.example: Etymology tells us that 'holy' originally meant 'whole' or 'complete.'

definitions.definition: Old English word meaning 'whole, complete, uninjured'; the root of the modern word 'holy.'
definitions.example: In Old English, a hālig person was someone who was whole and undamaged.
